THOUGHT: The presentation is classic for dermatomyositis: violaceous heliotrope/malar distribution on the face, Gottron papules over extensor hand joints, shawl/chest poikiloderma, characteristic nailfold capillary changes (dilated loops, dropout, ragged cuticles), and radiographic evidence of myositis. The markedly elevated type I interferon (IFN-β) and presence of anti–TIF‑1γ autoantibodies strongly support a dermatomyositis immune phenotype (dermatomyositis is an interferon-driven disease and anti‑TIF‑1γ is a well‑recognized myositis-specific autoantibody). Onset in childhood and multi‑system involvement point to juvenile dermatomyositis (JDM). Alternative diagnoses considered include cutaneous lupus erythematosus or overlap connective‑tissue disease (can be photosensitive and have cutaneous findings), inherited poikiloderma syndromes (Rothmund–Thomson, Kindler) that present with early photosensitivity and poikiloderma but lack the myositis and myositis‑specific antibodies, and mixed connective‑tissue disease/overlap myositis. Taken together, JDM (anti‑TIF‑1γ–positive) is by far the most likely diagnosis; the other entities are less consistent with the full constellation (particularly the myositis, myositis‑specific autoantibody, and interferon signature).

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Juvenile dermatomyositis (anti–TIF‑1γ–positive dermatomyositis)  
2) Dermatomyositis (other/overlap variant, adult-type/paraneoplastic-associated DM considered)  
3) Juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus / cutaneous lupus erythematosus (photosensitive lupus spectrum)  
4) Mixed connective‑tissue disease / overlap myositis (SSc–myositis or lupus–myositis overlap)  
5) Genetic poikiloderma syndromes (e.g., Rothmund–Thomson or Kindler syndrome)
